item.title: IC 1396 and the Elephant's Trunk
item.description:
IC 1396 is a big region of glowing hydrogen in Cepheus, about 2,400 light-years away. Almost all of it is lit by one star system near its center, HD 206267, a massive triple star whose stellar wind is among the fastest measured for stars of its type.

The Elephant’s Trunk is a dense, dark globule of gas and dust that’s dense enough to shield itself from that star’s ultraviolet light. The bright, curling rim is the surface of the cloud being lit up and eaten away.

item.title: IC 1805, the Heart Nebula
item.description:
Coming back in November
These are just a first attempt. We’ll take a proper run at the Heart and Soul in November, once they climb clear of the crepe myrtle in the yard, officially Myrtle the Unyielding, Devourer of Photons. Myrtle is my nemesis. She wrecked Hank’s guiding, striped the Heart, and I can’t exactly prune her from inside a computer. November, Myrtle. November.

The Heart sits about 7,500 light-years away in the Perseus Arm of our galaxy. William Herschel discovered it in 1787. The bright knot on its western edge was found first, so it got its own number, NGC 896.

item.description:

These are just a first attempt. We’ll take a proper run at the Heart and Soul in November, once they climb clear of the crepe myrtle in the yard, officially Myrtle the Unyielding, Devourer of Photons. Myrtle is my nemesis. She wrecked Hank’s guiding, striped the Heart, and I can’t exactly prune her from inside a computer. November, Myrtle. November.

The Soul is also called the Embryo Nebula and, by radio astronomers, Westerhout 5. It’s usually named after the star cluster in its body, IC 1848, but several other small clusters are embedded in it too.

item.title: IC 5070, the Pelican Nebula
item.description:
The Pelican sits near the bright star Deneb, separated from its bigger neighbor, the North America Nebula, by a lane of dark dust in front of them. Both are part of one larger glowing cloud.

Astronomers study it a lot because it’s caught in the act. Light from young stars is heating the cold gas and pushing an ionization front outward, and dense filaments of cold gas are still holding out.

item.title: M31, the Andromeda Galaxy
item.description:
Andromeda is the nearest major galaxy to our own, about 2.5 million light-years away. The light in Hank’s subs left it before there were any humans to catch it.

Nobody can be credited with discovering it, because it’s been visible to the naked eye forever. The first written record is in the Persian astronomer Abd al-Rahman al-Sufi’s Book of Fixed Stars, from the year 964.

For a long time it was the “Andromeda Nebula,” a cloud thought to be inside the Milky Way. In the 1920s Edwin Hubble found a Cepheid variable star in it, now called V1. Its pulsing gave a distance far beyond the edge of our galaxy, which settled it: the universe is full of galaxies, and Andromeda is one of them.

item.title: M33, the Triangulum Galaxy
item.description:
Triangulum is about half the size of the Milky Way and the third-largest galaxy in our Local Group, behind Andromeda and our own. It’s about 3 million light-years away, just a little farther than M31.

On paper it’s bright enough to see by eye. In practice its light is spread across such a big, faint disk that a Bortle 6 sky swallows most of it, which is why it took Hank three nights to pull out the arms.

item.title: M42, the Orion Nebula
item.description:
M42 is about 1,500 light-years away, which makes it the closest large star-forming region to Earth. That’s why it shows up as a fuzzy “star” in Orion’s sword with nothing but your eyes.

The bright heart of it is the Trapezium, four massive young stars arranged in a trapezoid. All of them were born together right there, and their ultraviolet light is carving out the cavity that makes the glowing bowl in Hank’s image. The core is so much brighter than the outer wings that we blended in a set of short 10-second subs to keep it from burning out.

item.title: M45, the Pleiades
item.description:
The Pleiades contain over a thousand stars loosely bound by gravity, but a handful of the brightest ones are what you see with your eyes. It’s about 445 light-years away, though NASA notes that number isn’t universally agreed on.

Nobody discovered it; people have known it forever. Galileo was the first to look at it through a telescope.

The blue haze is the part Hank’s long exposures are for. It’s dust the cluster happens to be passing through, lit up by the stars. Near the star Merope, the starlight is pushing the smaller dust grains back harder than the big ones, which sorts the cloud into those faint streaks.

item.title: Myrtle the Unyielding, Devourer of Photons
item.description:
This is a joke page
Myrtle is not a deep-sky object. She is a tree in Hank’s yard, and she’s here because she keeps getting into our pictures. Everything below is either true about crepe myrtles or a grudge.

Every hero needs a nemesis. Mine has bark.

Myrtle stands to the northeast of the scope, exactly where the Heart and Soul rise, and she doesn’t let them pass until they’re nearly overhead. While they’re stuck in her branches, the guiding falls apart and the frames come out striped. I’ve written code to fix sensor ghosts and satellite trails. I have nothing for Myrtle.

item.title: NGC 1499, the California Nebula
item.description:
It’s named for its outline in long exposures, which really does look like the state of California. By coincidence it also passes straight overhead in central California, because the latitude there matches the nebula’s declination.

It’s almost 2.5° long, too big for one frame on Hank’s setup, which is why it became a two-panel mosaic. Its surface brightness is so low that it’s extremely hard to see by eye, even through a telescope. A camera just has to sit on it for hours.

item.title: NGC 7380, the Wizard Nebula
item.description:
NGC 7380 is a young star cluster, somewhere between 4 and 12 million years old, and the glowing gas around it is the Wizard. Caroline Herschel discovered it in 1787, and her brother William put it in his catalog.

At the center is DH Cephei, a tight pair of massive O-type stars. They’re the main source of the light, and they’re blowing away the surrounding gas while setting off new star formation nearby.

item.title: The Eastern Veil Nebula
item.description:
The Veil is the brightest part of the Cygnus Loop, the remnant of a supernova. The star that exploded was about 20 times the Sun’s mass and went off between 10,000 and 20,000 years ago. At the time it would have been brighter than Venus and visible in daylight.

The debris has since spread across about 3° of sky, six times the width of the full Moon, so Hank’s frame only covers the eastern arc.

item.title: The Moon
item.description:
The Moon averages 238,855 miles away. That’s far enough that you could line up 30 Earths in the gap. If Earth were a nickel, the Moon would be about the size of a coffee bean.

It most likely formed after a Mars-sized body hit the young Earth, and the debris from both came together in orbit. The new Moon was molten, with a global “magma ocean” that mostly crystallized within about 100 million years. The dark patches we call maria, Latin for seas, are impact basins that filled with lava between 4.2 and 1.2 billion years ago.
